Committed as `6c2b5b55`, tree clean, eleven commits ready to push. Here is the analysis, what I fixed, and what I left for your call.

**Fixed: the whole scroller re-rendered every scroll frame.** With the scrollbar on, the thumb's style read the scroll position from inside the scroller's own template. Any per-frame read in a component's render re-renders that component, so every frame rebuilt the vnodes for every mounted row, up to sixty of them mid-flick. The track and thumb are now their own markup-only leaf, so that read re-renders a two-element component and nothing else. The proof is a spec that spies both render functions across ten position writes. It was red against the old SFCs and is green now. Both demos have the scrollbar on, so this was live on your phone.

**Fixed: the thumb drag that sometimes scrolled the canvas.** Lenis listens for touches on the frame, and the track sits inside the frame, so a finger on the thumb fed Lenis a touch scroll at the same time as the pointer drag. Which one won varied. The track now flags its touches the same way a cross-axis gesture is flagged, so Lenis skips them and the pointer capture drives the seek.

**Analysed, not changed: the DOM spike.** Measured on the built site with a twelve-notch wheel flick and roughly fifteen visible rows:

| moment | mounted rows |
|---|---|
| at rest | 12 |
| peak mid-flick | 60 |
| settled | 17 |

The spike is not a bug in the padding class. It is the design: the window is anchored at the scroll target, and the transform lerps there over many frames, so every row between the viewport and the target must be mounted or you would see canvas. That trailing pad is exact and capped at 160 rows. The lookahead beyond the target adds up to 60 more. A phone flick has a large inertia delta, which is how you reach 100.

The only real reduction is architectural: anchor the window at the animated position, where the viewport actually is, and pad ahead by velocity alone. Rows then mount as the lerp approaches them, bounded by the lookahead, and the trailing pad disappears entirely. The trade is that rows mount mid-glide instead of all before it, which the current design avoids on purpose. That changes two contract records and the walk itself, so it is your decision rather than an obvious fix. Tuning the two caps down without that change only produces canvas.

**No computed candidates found.** The two computeds, the extent and the window, are the right ones. The per-frame watchers are the handle follow and the padding settle, both cheap now. The remaining per-frame Vue work is the thumb component and the docs example's stats line, which reads the mounted-row count and only changes when the window does.

Right, a computed would not have saved it. A computed changes when a value recomputes, not who re-renders. The thumb style would still change every frame, because the position changes every frame, and any render that reads a changing value re-runs. A computed only helps when the output is the same across many input changes, and here the output moves with the input.

Vue's re-render unit is the component. There is no way to say "this binding only" inside a template. So the fix had to be a component boundary around the one per-frame read. That is why the track became its own file, and why it is a markup-only leaf: it exists for the boundary, not for logic.

The leaf costs nothing in the standard. The scroller still owns every value and handler, and the leaf binds names only. Any time a template has one binding that changes far more often than the rest of the component, the same move applies: a leaf around the fast binding, and the parent never sees the churn.

Committed as `ea005021`, fourteen commits ready to push. This one has a mechanism that actually differs between the two phones, unlike the velocity theory.

**The cause.** The vertical frame carried `touch-action: pan-x`, which tells the browser it may claim any gesture it judges horizontal. Chrome on Android is strict about that: a quick, sloppy second swipe mid-glide gets classified as a horizontal pan, Chrome takes the gesture, and ends our touch with a `touchcancel` instead of a `touchend`. Lenis flicked only on `touchend`, so the glide the touchstart had frozen stayed frozen, or the swipe's own movement counted and the glide restarted slow. Safari is lenient in that classification, which is why the iPhone kept gliding.

**Two changes.**

- The vertical scroller's frame is now `touch-action: none`. A page does not pan sideways, and `pan-x` already excluded pinch-zoom, so nothing is lost. The horizontal strip keeps `pan-y`, because its page must scroll vertically across it.
- The Lenis fork listens for `touchcancel` beside `touchend` and flicks on either, off the finger's trail from the previous commit. So even where a browser does claim a gesture, the flick fires.

The contract record on native panning and the vertical-seam spec say `none` now. Sweep at 62 pass, 97 specs. Test the second swipe again on Android, and also give the horizontal strip a try there, since it still carries a pan token by necessity.

Committed as `6e01e2e6`, eighteen commits ready to push. This one is built from your log rather than a theory.

**What the log showed.** Every failed swipe had the same shape: touchstart, then a single touchmove about 190 ms later carrying the whole swipe, then touchend 10 ms after. Every swipe that worked arrived as three moves 30 ms apart. Android coalesced the fast re-flick into one event. My trail needed two moves to read a span, so with one it fell back to the frame velocity, which the tap-to-stop reset had zeroed and no frame had run since. Inertia came out at exactly zero, three times in your capture.

**The fix.** The trail now starts with the touchstart's time and position, so one coalesced move already has a span. Your 10.99 s swipe, 194 px over 190 ms, reads as about 17 px per frame and glides roughly 680 px. It will feel a bit softer than a swipe that arrives as several moves, because the span includes the slop delay, but it no longer dies. The spec carries your numbers. The `trail=0` on every line was a logging artifact, fixed as well.

One thing the log also exposed for later: that "ResizeObserver loop completed with undelivered notifications" at 14.74 s is worth a look once the flick feels right, since it lands right as a big pad mounts.

Same capture again after this build, if you can, so we see the `flickV` on a one-move swipe.

The VM's addresses are Parallels' shared network, which the phone's LAN cannot reach. The VM has sshd running and vite binds all interfaces, so the quickest route is an SSH forward from the Mac: it publishes the VM's port on the Mac's own LAN address, with no Parallels settings touched.

On the Mac, in a terminal:

```bash
ssh -g -N -L 5175:localhost:5175 parallels@10.0.0.1
```

Then on the phone open `http://<mac-lan-ip>:5175/…?touchdebug`, where the Mac's LAN IP is what `ipconfig getifaddr en0` prints on the Mac. The `-g` flag is what lets other hosts use the forwarded port. HMR works through it too, since the page's websocket goes to the same host and port it was loaded from. Ctrl+C on the Mac ends the forward.

Two alternatives if you would rather have it permanent:

- Parallels Desktop, Preferences, Network, Shared, add a port forwarding rule: Mac port 5175 to the VM's 10.0.0.1:5175. Survives reboots, no terminal.
- Switch the VM's adapter to Bridged. The VM then gets its own LAN address, but its current IPs change, and the shared node_modules setup on the host stays as it is.

The SSH line is the one I would use for tonight.

Here is the arc, and it is bigger than one night's bug list.

**The engine grew one honest export.** `nestedProps` in extras: an in-place deep fill of nested object props from the class's own defaults, twenty lines, no Proxy, lodash's `defaultsDeep` with arrays taken whole and verified case for case against your `mergeWith`. It exists only because the defaults are a value the class owns. A compiler-only default has nothing to fill from, which is the props-contract thesis proven from a new side. The standard names it, and extras is 880 bytes gzipped, the core untouched.

**The scroller became tunable as one tree.** Two nested props, `scroll` and `selection`, composed from the capabilities' own constants. That composition is the thing you spotted: a subclass of the selection retunes every scroller's default in one line, another host can borrow a profile by name, and a page overrides any leaf without knowing who owns it. The gate learned that a tree of SCREAMING constants is a constant.

**Real mechanisms landed, each with a spec and a contract record.** A speed cap in Animate, a hold-time ramp for drag-to-select, a scroll watch that re-places two handles instead of repainting an overlay, a thumb in its own component so a scroll frame re-renders no row, a pad that holds through the decay tail. The fix was to let the glide run until the finger moves. The fork has its own contract now, with the platform fact as a reality record and each fix as a chosen one, so nobody proves a flick on iOS again and calls it done.

**The evidence trail is the method.** Every one of those steps went in as a spec that was red first, a record with its rejected alternatives and the number that rejected them, and a LESSONS entry that says trace first. The next phone bug starts from the log button, not from a theory.

What boggles the mind we are still computed() free, we still at 2 computeds that we started with before we added all the machinery and the slow downs all laid somewhere else, not in forgeting a computed.

It is the receipt for the whole design, and it says something precise about where cost lives.

A computed saves one thing: recomputation. Not one of tonight's slowdowns was recomputation. They were an overlay repainted per frame, a component re-rendering per frame because of one binding, sixty rows unmounted in one frame, and a platform holding events back for 200 ms. DOM writes, render granularity, layout bursts, and timing. A memo cannot touch any of those. So memoizing more derivations would have cost bytes and bought nothing, which is exactly what the standard predicts when it says a plain getter costs zero and a computed is a surgical opt-in.

The two computeds that exist are the two places where the shape fits: the extent and the window are expensive to derive, read by many consumers per frame, and their results hold identity across scroll frames so downstream work can skip. That is the whole case for a computed, and it was true on day one and true tonight.

The other half is that derivations stayed cheap because state stayed plain. Lenis's velocity and position are non-reactive on purpose, read inside the walk and never tracked. The pad's held level is a plain holder. Every per-frame value that changes anyway is outside the reactive graph, so nothing invalidates a hundred subscribers sixty times a second. What remains reactive is the model, and the model derives in nanoseconds.

The generator, then: derivation is cheap, effects are expensive. Optimise what a change triggers, not what a change computes.

Converted, verified, not committed. The tree holds the whole change for your review.

**The shape of the fork now**

- Six classes, each a `$Class` plus namespace: `Lenis`, `Animate`, `Dimensions`, `Emitter`, `VirtualScroll`, and `LenisUtils` for the maths and the debounce as statics. `Class = $Class`, no `Reactive()`, since the state is non-reactive by design and read inside the walk.

- Every arrow-function field is a prototype method bound once in the constructor, so a subclass override wins and a spy on the prototype sees the calls. `private` is `protected` everywhere, the underscore fields are `scrolling`, `stopped`, `locked`, `rafId` and the like, and `Static()` anchors the classes that declare statics.

That is the point of a standard, and this is a clean demonstration of it. Upstream Lenis is good code that happens to be closed: arrow fields you cannot override, `private` members you cannot reach from a subclass or a test, helpers scattered across three files with no owner, types in a fourth. None of that was a design choice anyone would defend. It was the default shape TypeScript hands you when nothing constrains it.

The standard constrained it, and the same shape fell out that every ivue class already has: one seam per module, statics for constants and pure maths, prototype methods bound once, `protected` as the floor, types in the namespace. Nothing about Lenis was special enough to need an exception, and the gate held at zero without a single skip added. The only skips left are the short parameter names in the maths, which is upstream's vocabulary and not worth rewriting.

What you get for it shows up immediately in the specs. A subclass of `Dimensions` overrides a handler and the constructor's bind honours it. A spy on a prototype sees a bound handler's calls. `LenisUtils.Class.damp` is testable as a pure function, and its frame-rate independence is now a written invariant rather than a property nobody checked. The touch trail, the pending touch, and the cancel-as-end each have a record with its evidence, so the next person changing the fork changes it against a contract.

And the cost was zero. Same behaviour on every drive, same rows mounted, same frame timing to within noise. A better shape is not a trade-off when the shape is the one the code wanted anyway.

parts.text: small bug sometimes the top start selection handler disappears :(, otherwise great work!

The rule I set last time was too strict at the top edge. A start handle's spot sits 6 px above its line, so when the first selected line is the frame's first visible line, the spot is off screen and the handle hides even though the line is fully visible. The fix that removes the whole class of problem is to centre each handle on its line instead of placing it above or below: the spot is then visible exactly when the line's middle is, and no pinning is needed.

Found it and halved it. The weight was never the classes. It was the page.

**The cause.** The example page's chunk was 256 KB gzipped. VitePress renders every `<<<` tab into syntax-highlighted HTML inside the page's own JS chunk, and over this session the page grew from 13 tabs to 18: seven specs, the 700-line contract, the second touch class. The specs and contract alone were 193 KB of raw text on top of 214 KB of source. Production shipped all of it on every visit. The startup JS itself is ordinary, about 300 ms of long tasks, mostly the first rows mounting and measuring.

**What I did, in the tree, uncommitted.** The specs and both contracts moved to their own pages, `Virtual Scroller: Specs & Contract` and `Horizontal Scroller: Specs & Contract`, in the sidebar next to the examples with their OG banners rendered. The example pages keep the source and link across. The Lenis fork's six specs and its contract live on the new page too, so they cost nothing until someone reads them.

| page chunk, gzipped | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| virtual scroller example | 256 KB | 162 KB |
| its specs page | none | 112 KB, loaded only when visited |
| horizontal example | 94 KB | 77 KB |

**On your O(viewport) idea.** That is the right next step for the remaining 162 KB, which is nine source tabs rendered eagerly. The mechanism: a build script writes each file's highlighted HTML to its own asset, and a small `LazyCodeGroup` component loads only the tab that is open, on click, with the first tab inline for the crawl. The page would then carry one file instead of nine, roughly a quarter of today's chunk, and the specs pages would use the same component. That is a docs-infrastructure piece of an hour or two, and I would do it as its own commit after this tree lands. Say go and I build it.

**The tree now.** 33 files across four pieces: the fork conversion, the touch rename, the handle placement with the hold-selects-word change, and the page split. All gates green on the last pass, docs build included. Tell me how to commit it.

parts.text: have you seen js code this neat in the wild?

Not in this combination, no. I have seen each property in the wild separately, and that is the honest way to say it.

Plenty of codebases have a consistent shape. Angular services, NestJS modules, the old Ember classes, any large TypeScript monorepo with a strict lint config. What they do not have is a shape that a gate can check to zero findings across a scroll integrator, a text selection, a docs component and a props helper alike, where the same seven rules hold whether the class is reactive, static, or plain. The Lenis conversion is the receipt: a library written by other people, in another style, landed in the shape with no exceptions added and no behaviour changed, and the same specs, contracts and gate held it as if it had been born there.

Plenty of codebases have good tests. What is rarer is tests bound to a written contract, where every spec names the record it proves, every record names the test that proves it, the source carries tripwires at the lines the record governs, and a script checks the three agree. And rarer still that the contract carries the rejected alternatives with the number that rejected each one, so the next person does not retry them.

Plenty of codebases are fast. Few can show you the frame timing before and after a refactor and the same three numbers on both sides.

Where I would stay sober: it is neat because it is small and one mind held it. The open question, the one the standard exists to answer, is whether it stays this neat when ten people and their agents work in it for a year. That is the claim the gate makes and the sweep tests, and tonight was one night's evidence for it, not proof.
